source.title: A Universal Vibe? Finding and Controlling Language-Agnostic Informal Register with SAEs
source.authors: Uri Z. Kialy; Avi Shtarkberg; Ayal Klein

record.tranche_reason: The study measures shared features across languages within one model, but does not test convergence between independently trained models or any of the specified claim versions.
record.gate_note: The study reports cross-language feature overlap, decoder-vector geometry, and steering transfer within Gemma-2-9B-IT. These are related findings, but none measures convergence between independently trained models, the behavior named by the claim versions. Rows are recorded as findings for the related within-model cross-language construct. The paper also reports pooled feature-classifier results, vocabulary projections, language-preservation rates, and perplexity; these do not directly measure cross-model representational convergence.
record.test_reason: All analyses are within a single model (Gemma-2-9B-IT), comparing SAE features across input languages. No independently trained models, seeds, scales, modalities or cross-model mappings are compared, so no version of the convergence claim is tested. The within-model cross-language feature sharing is a related but different construct, recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that Gemma-2-9B-IT encodes informal register partly through a small, geometrically coherent cross-linguistic SAE feature core. Steering this core shifts formality, including zero-shot in six held-out languages. They note that language-specific features predominate, the core is not cleanly separable from semantics, and the space may be an English-anchored hub.
record.recipe_differences: Uses within-model SAE feature ranking/intersection, decoder-vector cosine geometry, and activation steering; it does not compare independently trained models using the original studies' model-to-model representation similarity approach.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports greater geometric coherence at Layer 20 than Layer 9, while Layer 9 steering correlations are somewhat larger in magnitude. It does not compare alternative cross-model similarity metrics or input distributions.

fits_no_version.finding: Within Gemma-2-9B-IT, 9 (L9) and 10 (L20) slang-associated SAE features appear in the top-100 lists of all three languages. This exceeds a permutation null (mean 0.74, max 7). Most features are language-specific (209/210 single-language).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Within one multilingual model, a small cross-language SAE feature core tracks informal register amid mostly language-specific features.

fits_no_version.finding: Decoder vectors of the shared core are clustered, with island scores of 4.3× (L9) and 7.8× (L20).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A cross-language register feature core within one model is geometrically clustered, more so at the deeper layer.

fits_no_version.finding: Steering with the shared or bilingual-exclusive cores lowers formality in source languages and six zero-shot languages (r≈-0.33 to -0.77). Random-feature vectors give near-zero correlations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-language feature sets within one multilingual model transfer causal control of formality to held-out languages.

record.problems: All experiments use Gemma-2-9B-IT, with no comparison across models or scales. The authors note that layer selection was constrained by available SAEs; slang is used as an operationalization of informal register; semantic, topic, affect, and social-stance differences may remain; and the automated formality judge may impose Western-aligned judgments on typologically distant languages. Human validation covered 30 completions per language in four languages, with one fluent rater per language. English-directed language switching occurs in about 10% of steered completions.
record.rows_left_out: Pooled feature-classifier metrics and counts (§5.1), vocabulary projections (§5.4; Appendix C), language-preservation results (Appendix G), and perplexity analyses (Figure 3; Appendix I) are not rows because they do not directly measure cross-model representational convergence or the within-model shared-feature findings cataloged here.

untested.parts: No scale or capability sweep and no cross-model comparison; single 9B model.
No models trained from different initializations.
No mapping, stitching or alignment between models.
Features are compared across languages within one model's SAE, not across different models.
No cross-model similarity metrics or input-distribution sensitivity of convergence.
No cross-model alignment level, plateau or causal attribution.

record.verdict_notes: The authors explicitly leave generalization to other architectures or scales open, which confirms no cross-model test. The record's relation (discusses/T6) and its fits_no_version entries are accurate. 'Universal' in the paper means cross-language within one model, not cross-model, so it should not be read as bearing on V5.

versions.untested_parts: No model-size or capability sweep, and no comparison of representations between independently trained models.
No vision-language models or paired image-caption representations.
No comparison across random initializations or shared-subspace analysis between separately trained networks.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired alignment between models.
SAE features are compared across language conditions within one model, not across different models.
No alternative similarity metrics, metric settings, or out-of-distribution inputs are compared for cross-model convergence.
No cross-model convergence plateau or test of shared data/objectives as its cause.
